We propose a novel approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to create realistic upsampled video frames from low-resolution inputs, using only a few high-quality frames as training data.  By exploiting the spatial and temporal connections in video frames, our approach achieves remarkable results without needing vast datasets for training.  We test our approach on two challenging tasks: removing motion blur and enhancing video quality.  Our results show that our approach matches the performance of models trained on large datasets.  Additionally, we introduce a framework that generates diverse video scenarios from single samples, allowing us to conduct extensive experiments with realistic data.  By demonstrating our method's effectiveness on data generated in this way, we highlight the potential benefits of this approach for large-scale video super-resolution projects.  We have our approach and generated datasets available for download at https://github.com/xtar111/video-sr.

  1. A video super-resolution approach that uses a very limited number of high-quality frames for training.

  2. An innovative use of generative adversarial networks to create realistic upsampled video frames from low-resolution inputs.

We use the language of bilinear forms to provide an arithmetic interpretation of the principal component analysis (PCA), establishing that PCA corresponds to maximizing the variance of a bilinear form, subject to an identity constraint.  This interpretation serves as the foundation for an algorithm that allows us to enumerate all possible PCA solutions for a given matrix size, thereby determining the frequencies of variances within a matrix set.  Frequency measures then form the basis for a tensor factorization method, called the frequency-aware singular value decomposition (FA-sVDec).  By combining the PCAs of adjacent sub-matrices, the FA-sVDec can reconstruct the original matrix, demonstrating that this approach has computational efficiency benefits over traditional SVD for certain matrices.  A further analysis indicates that matrix factors exhibit a hierarchical relationship, enabling us to capture the global structure of a matrix by combining its local frequency patterns.  Building upon this understanding, a method for iteratively applying different FA-sVDecs along a matrix row or column has been developed, showcasing its application in modeling dynamic, heterogeneous data networks.  A software tool, called the Tensor Playground, is also provided to support the exploration and manipulation of matrices using the frequency-aware approach.  The work presented here integrates theoretical concepts and practical implementations for matrix understanding, while introducing the concept of a tensor melody that captures the unique harmonic structure of a matrix.  By extending the idea of unique frequencies to multiple harmonics, the tensor melody provides a powerful tool for discriminating between similar matrices and provides a novel application of the frequency-aware approach.  This research also introduces the idea of harmonics collision that occurs when two matrices share a common frequency, but have an overlapping set of harmonics.  It is shown that matrices experiencing harmonics collision due to a common column will have a specific relationship, implying that frequency collision has practical implications for matrix rotation and composition.  A classification of matrix relationships based on their harmonics is proposed and a method to compute the frequency spectrum of a matrix is described.  The work also presents the concept of an harmonic database that contains matrices with specific frequency characteristics, while providing the implementation of an algorithm that generates all possible PCAs for a given matrix size and frequency spectrum.  The frequency database provides an efficient means to match matrices against their descriptors. The field of object annotation has been largely unstudied, with little consideration given to the task of annotating new objects not present in the training data.  This work introduces a subtask called one-shot object annotation, where the goal is to annotate an object in a testing image given that the model has seen the object in question during training, but nowhere else.  One-shot object annotation can be seen as a partial-to-partial mapping problem between images seen during training and those in the testing set.  The model learns a representation that facilitates this mapping by exploiting the relational data available during training, allowing it to exploit existing labels.  The field of object annotation benefits from this work, while the findings also contribute to a broader understanding of how models retain information about objects they have been trained on, with implications for future research into object relations, a task made possible by this work's one-shot object annotation task.  The work includes methods for annotating objects in images not present in the training data, demonstrating that a model pre-trained for object detection can be fine-tuned to exploit existing labels, with results showing that a model trained on one-shot annotation tasks achieves the same accuracy as a model trained on a large dataset with comprehensive annotations. While most existing studies have focused on solving multi-class classification problems, our work aims to address a distinct challenge in computer vision - the Few-Shot (F-S) classification problem. In this problem, a model is presented with data from just one to five individual classes for both training and fine-tuning. Our research introduces a novel approach that leverages a separate generation adversarial network, generating not only the main class but also any additional supporting classes found in the data, with the advantage of significantly reducing the required training dataset size. By utilizing this approach on the CIFAR-100 and tiny-ImageNet datasets, we have achieved state-of-the-art few-shot classification performance. Furthermore, we have also introduced an alternative method that achieves comparable results without the need for an additional generation adversarial network, resulting in a uniscale framework that facilitates ease in interpreting model decisions, providing explicit semantic evidence for correct classifications. This is particularly beneficial in F-S applications where data distribution varies substantially. Additionally, we have introduced an efficient technique called the Reverse Reconstruction Classifier, which generates evidence in the form of a single class label, enabling the model to focus on distinguishing one specific class from all others, leading to enhanced performance. This approach has achieved superior results when compared to conventional techniques such as prototype-based methods, affording a 6.3% improvement in accuracy when evaluating models on the CIFAR-100 F-S benchmark. research has focused on utilizing various signals such as WiFi, Bluetooth, ultrasound, light, magnetic fields, and radio frequency signals for localization purposes.  Each of these approaches employs a single signal type and utilizes different techniques including range finding, area division methods, and calibration-free methods for indoor localization.  In contrast, a novel approach involves utilizing multiple signal types including radio frequency, ultrasound, light, and magnetic fields to improve accuracy and reduce the dispersion of localization results.  These signals were sent from a range of devices including routers, ultrasound devices, LED bulbs, and smart plugs that comprise the indoor localization system.  The proposed system includes a protocol designed to minimize energy consumption while providing accurate localization results.  Experiments conducted in an office room and a larger apartment setting demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding high accuracy with low data dispersion.  Furthermore, the system exhibits robust performance despite the complex nature of indoor environments.  Compared to utilizing a single signal type, the proposed system shows improved accuracy and lower data dispersion.  In addition, the energy-efficient protocol enables cost-effective monitoring and indoor location-aware services.  Experimental results indicate that the system can support up to 10 users per room, offering practical applications for monitoring and location-aware systems in indoor settings.  Furthermore, reducing the transmission frequency and duration in the protocol demonstrates energy consumption reduction, although at the expense of slightly increased localization error.  This approach has potential for combined use of multiple signal types including WiFi, Bluetooth, and magnetic fields in future location-aware systems.  Experimental data has been made available for the proposed protocol and reference models at <https://github.com/ahmadv1/FCRF>.

This study delves into the technical aspects of implementing SPS using a simple SPS device that interacts with a two-mode entangled light state. We demonstrate the efficiency of this device by showing the effectiveness of single-photon subtraction in a scenario involving entangled light states. Furthermore, we examine the efficacy of this process when there is loss in the SPS device, and we find that entanglement is preserved after the single-photon subtraction process, even with device loss. While traditional methods tie the probability model to a specific parametric distribution, modern approaches allow for non-parametric models, yet often overlook the inherent uncertainty in the underlying distribution. Our own contribution, the Bayesian Non-parametric Distribution Learning (BNDDL), mitigates this limitation by inferring both the underlying distribution and the uncertainty inherent to it. We have applied an extension of this method to understand the underlying distribution of physical action types within the Music21 dataset, a comprehensive collection of musical scores. By utilizing the Vinyals et al. action recognition system as a preprocessor, we have been able to investigate the inherent uncertainty in the distribution of these action types. Our results demonstrate that the underlying distribution of action types is not uniformly random, but rather exhibits distinct peaks in probability, with certain actions being more probable than others. Furthermore, we have observed that actions which are more probable have a stronger connection to the object they are acting upon, as indicated by p-values less than 0.01 in nearly all cases. Additionally, our analysis reveals that actions with a higher probability of occurring are more likely to be involved in the program's inference, as evidenced by a high correlation between the probability of an action and the likelihood of it being part of the program's inferred set, which holds true for all types of objects being acted upon. Furthermore, we compare this result to recent findings on the binary multiple-access channel. Additionally, this paper presents the results of a Monte Carlo simulation that verify our theoretical findings. This research also provides a starting point for analyzing other forms of multiple-access channels that involve the superposition of signals. Inferring hidden states from just one previous time step, like in RNN, is an oversimplification of how we internally represent sequences.  To address these limitations, existing research on high-order state inference has been hindered by the need to fit multiple parameters for each time step and state, making models difficult to train and express.  Through a novel compact parameterization suitable for High-Order RNNs, our work overcomes these challenges.  Our Compact Multi-Layer RNN design fits multiple time steps and states with the L1 and L2 regularization techniques, and we have found a suitable layer compaction method that works well with both RNN and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) cells.  Our model's performance outperforms standard RNN and LSTM networks on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating equivalent or improved performance while achieving a significant reduction in parameters.  Ultimately, our Compact Multi-Layer RNNs offer a balanced combination of hidden state inference capability, parameter efficiency, and ease of training, making them an attractive alternative to traditional RNNs for sequence-to-sequence applications. We demonstrate that achieving this level of robustness comes with a significant computational cost, surpassing any known polynomial-time optimization method. Specifically, unless NP has a pseudo-polynomial time approximation factor theorem, there's no polynomial-time algorithm that can efficiently handle a streaming adversarially robust version of a commonly recognized problem, THE SEMI-SUM PROBLEM. This problem involves estimating the total value of a dataset, which contains integers within a bounded range, by making a single pass through the data. Even with a strong assumption - having access to a near-optimal solution without the stream - there's no polynomial-time algorithm that can efficiently handle a streaming semi-sum problem with an arbitrary bound. However, the algorithm we present does provide useful insights, as it yields a semi-sum estimate with an o(1)-regret on a bounded range dataset, using O(~(log n)^2) space where n represents the number of data points. This achievement holds under a reasonable distribution assumption and an adversary that manipulates the data with a limited effort, specifically ~O(1/n^2) multiplicative factor. This accomplishment builds upon previous work involving streaming semi-sum problems and provides a computational complexity theory perspective that contrasts with a recent result involving a robust Freiman 2-theorem. Additionally, we highlight an extension to a multivariate semi-sum problem and an application to a robust streaming estimate problem with a non-negative range. This research also includes an illustration of a simple streaming problem that is both computationally hard and robust. This work accelerates research into streaming robust optimization and may influence development of robust streaming algorithms. Although we present an adverse outcome for a particular class of algorithms, we also demonstrate an effective streaming algorithm that addresses an alternative definition of robustness, specifically robustness to a data skew caused by a streaming order. This research provides a starting point and a set of open questions for a broader study of streaming robust optimization. Specifically, we invite colleagues to examine the intricacies of a streaming robust semi-sum problem with an unbounded data range. This research was a collaborative effort involving Yufei Cao, an undergraduate student at Harvard University, and the last two authors. It includes an extension to a streaming robust count-sketch problem that was an independent contribution of the last two authors along with David Zhang. This research also includes an illustration of a simple streaming problem that was an independent contribution of Grigorescu,

This approach is particularly well-suited for a wide range of complex structures across multiple frequency bands, including microwave and optical components, radar systems, and satellite structures requiring frequency-sorted CMS. This method overcomes previous limitations  in win-loss optimization by allowing for the representation of maximum distances  between locations, rather than simply upper bounds on distances. We demonstrate  the efficacy of this approach through computational tests and show that it can  provide more efficient solutions when compared to standard methods for small-scale  instances. The time spent on  optimizing the assignment and the reversal step varies, but typically falls within  a range of a few seconds to around a minute. The number of reversals required,  on the other hand, usually lies between 10 and 1,000, though in some cases it may  exceed 10,000. The number of locations in the tested instances ranged from 50  to 500, with the maximum possible distance parameter ranging from 100 to 1,000.  Due to the high cost of computing the optimal assignment in each iteration,  the proposed algorithm has been parallelized to improve performance. The developed  approach may be applied to other types of location-based problems, such as the  multi-capacitated facility location problem. Further research is needed to fully  parallelize the algorithm and to explore its applicability to these other types  of problems. The developed approach  has been tested and evaluated on a set of synthetic uncapacitated facility  location test instances, with modifications to accommodate maximum distance  specifications. The results show that the first-to-last win-loss optimization  algorithm delivers superior or comparable solution quality to the standard  closeness and p-median methods, as measured through objective function  value and fraction optimality. The proposal to use win-loss optimization  for facility location problems is a direct extension of the research presented  in Ahn and Gelfand (Comput Oper Res 38(11):2939-2949, 2011), where this  algorithm was applied to a similar problem type, but with upper bound distance  specifications

  influence of memory on dynamics, with the Rouse theory being a logical
  extension of this model in the absence of memory effects. Despite this, the
  Rouse model has limitations in accurately representing memory-driven dynamics.
  Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the extended Rouse model can be
  approximated using a non-Markovian Fokker-Planck equation, with this
  approximation being feasible even in systems with significant memory
  contributions. Analytical solutions to the Rouse model can be used to
  determine fractional time and interaction coefficients in the
  non-Markovian Fokker-Planck equation, making it possible to predict
  memory-driven effects on polymer dynamics through analytical means. With this
  approach, we examine the impact of memory on the time-dependent mean squared
  displacement of Rouse chains and compare our results to Monte Carlo
  simulations. Our analysis shows that memory retards the free-diffusion stage
  and significantly affects the sub-diffusive regime, with the memory effects
  increasing with the memory times and fraction of monomers influenced.  Overall,

charging infrastructure deployment. To optimize this process, we need to balance multiple key factors: investments in charging stations, overall electricity usage, and the performance of the transportation network. To tackle this complex problem, we propose a mathematical model that reframes charging infrastructure investment as a mean-field control issue. By leveraging the mean-field concept, we can split the model into two more manageable components: one represents the population of drivers with similar intentions, modeled as a control system; the other involves the spatial distribution of drivers, modeled as a transport equation. We derive a set of optimal control systems that mirror the population of drivers, based on their initial distribution and the performance of the transportation network. By using these models in a numerical example, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in optimizing charging infrastructure investment compared to a random investment approach. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the mean-field approach outperforms the random strategy in terms of social welfare, and the performance improves as the population of drivers increases. However, the benefit also increases the time it takes to reach an optimal outcome. To address this, we consider a slower-moving mean-field model, which yields a more exploitable subproblem; this enables us to integrate the algorithm efficiently, resulting in better convergence. By applying the faster-moving model to a larger-scale network and the smaller model to a network with nodes of varying importance, we have conducted additional numerical tests. The findings suggest that the method we present can be used to optimize charging infrastructure investment efficiently, even in real-world scenarios. Finally, we highlight potential extensions to our research, such as integrating alternative transportation modes and addressing stationary energy storage optimisation. These criteria, which are based on the principle of leptoquark self-coupling, provide a more comprehensive framework for the examination of the data. As a result, accurate load forecasting is crucial for optimizing pricing, inventory, and customer services, thereby contributing to the overall stability of the electricity infrastructure. Nevertheless, forecasting electricity consumption poses significant difficulties, primarily because it is a transcription of complex human behavior linked to various factors, including temperature, lighting, and other weather conditions. Utilities and electricity providers typically utilize conventional methods like time series analysis and classical statistical techniques for this purpose. However, given the nonlinear nature of electricity consumption patterns, these traditional approaches often yield suboptimal results. Consequently, there is a pressing need for innovative forecasting methods that can learn from data and replicate the complex relationships present in consumption patterns. Given the advances made in artificial intelligence, neural networks appear particularly well-suited for this purpose, given their capacity to detect non-linear patterns and replicate complex relationships present in data. This paper introduces an approach that combines classical meteorological forecasts with artificial intelligence-powered load forecasts, utilizing historical consumption patterns and real-time operational data to train the models. Although results vary across test cases, our proposal demonstrates improved forecasting accuracy when compared to industry-standard methods, highlighting the potential of this approach to enhance operational efficiency and reduce costs associated with inaccurate forecasts. Furthermore, this approach is flexible and adaptable to different datasets with varying characteristics, thereby providing a viable solution for utilities and electricity providers seeking to enhance their forecasting capabilities. non-cylindrical shape. Existing studies have shown that incorporating more

attempts to parameterize the tube method using the surface area and flow

ances and are typically modeled using sequence-to-sequence techniques.  These models are trained to transform the previous conversation history into a single utterance.  However, real-world conversations often consist of multiple speaking turns with varying speaker roles.  A proposed approach to addressing this issue involves the use of graph neural networks to represent conversations graphically and model speaker roles.  Our research builds upon this idea by separating the utterance representation from the model's primary graph representation.  A proposed model uses a series of interconnected nodes to represent the utterances in a conversation. These additional nodes are positioned based on the utterances' roles in the conversation and are trained via a proposed scoring mechanism. Our research demonstrates that a theoretical model of microwave-like interactions between x-ray photons and electron fields allows for a simplified description of this scenario, providing a framework for future optimization and design of FEL facilities to produce tailored, sample-driven x-ray pulses. Specifically, we show that a one-pass photoelectron spectrum can be factored into an array of cross-correlated components, including their initial, bulk electron components, electrons scattered onto an upper energy band, and those that undergo further interactions, resulting in an energy-dispersed spectrum. To produce a pulse with an extended duration, we propose a simple strategy based on this decomposition, involving the manipulation of a few key parameters, such as energy dispersion, an energy threshold, and a soft-photon filter. computer vision, the field has yet to achieve a comprehensive understanding of image recognition.  Current approaches primarily rely on empirical theories, leveraging sophisticated architectures and extensive training data to implicitly capture the underlying principles of image recognition.  These methods fail to provide transparent or easily interpretable results, making it impossible to deduce the underlying vision and perception abilities from the output.  To address this knowledge gap, we present the Hypersphere Model, a groundbreaking framework that not only produces accurate image recognition results but also allows us to explicitly parse the underlying vision and perception aspects by reducing the classification task to a set of disjoint hyper spherical surfaces.  By transforming each high-dimensional feature vector into a one-dimensional angle, we can capture the relative position of objects in images, thereby gaining insight into the underlying vision and perception.  Furthermore, our model includes a built-in mechanism to identify the minimum number of necessary features required for each class, resulting in significant data compression, and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets while matching the performance of mainstream models in extensive evaluation tests.  By decomposing the classification task into disjoint hyperspheres, the model is able to extract unique attributes from each class, thereby achieving superior performance in semantic feature selection and incremental learning evaluations.  The code for the Hypersphere Model is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yl-19/Hypersphere-Model.  The model's trained parameters are hosted on Baidu Cloud at https://pan.baidu.com/cloud/link/123456.  The dataset generators and evaluation scripts are also provided.  With the Hypersphere Model, we are able to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying vision and perception that governs image recognition from a theoretical perspective.  By leveraging this insight, we can derive a set of intuitive and visually interpretable meta-attributes that capture the semantic aspects of objects in images.  By combining the Hypersphere Model's superior recognition performance with its ability to extract meta-attributes, we can accelerate the development of real-world vision applications, by providing a means to interpret and understand the underlying vision and perception that governs image recognition.   However, determining the most efficient path that connects two equilibrium 
  states remains a significant challenge. Here, we introduce an unsupervised 
  optimization framework to find the fastest path by exploring a wide range 
  of competing free energies under the constraint of a fixed total computational 
  budget. This approach yields the most cost-effective path for calculating 
  free energies and can be applied to model energies that cannot be simulated 
  directly, thanks to an inner loop that utilizes a reduced representation 
  without a clear energy expression, such as in deep neural network potentials. 
  We demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of our method in locating the 
  minimum-action path even when starting from an arbitrary initial condition, 
  by comparing predicted and observed thermodynamic behaviors in molecular 
  expansions, and by evaluating the accuracy of various atomic structures 
  predicted using a deep potential with and without this optimization 
  framework. Furthermore, we show that employing the unsupervised optimizer 
  yields a significant computational benefit without additional computational 
  expense, resulting in a substantial reduction in computational time and 
  resources needed for free energy calculations under the same level of 
  accuracy. This technique is particularly beneficial for large datasets and 
  can be seamlessly integrated with existing Hamiltonian path metropolis 
  algorithms to enhance the accuracy of thermodynamic property estimations. 
  By providing an efficient means of locating the minimum-action path, this 
  method can also be employed to improve the performance of neural network 
  models through a supervised learning scheme that leverages the optimized 
  paths. This unsupervised optimizer has the potential to be applied to 
  other Markov State Models, such as diffusion maps and transition-based 
  methods, for further improvement in their accuracy and computation 
  efficiency. The code for this study has been made available on a GitHub

To address this limitation, this research introduces a new approach based on semantic vector space, where we enhance the flexible structure of BERT-like language models by incorporating the latent meanings of words as learnable vectors.  By doing so, we leverage the semantic relationships between words to prevent the disconnection of word clusters within the vector space, resulting in a model that can efficiently mix word representations to fill in the lexical gaps.  To realize this vision, we develop a proposal-based training method that allows us to manipulate the word meanings within the vector space, minimizing the distance between the target word's neighbors and the mixed word representations.  By demonstrating improved performance on zero-shot and few-shot learning tasks for 19 out-of-domain classification datasets, our results show that our approach surpasses standard BERT in accuracy by an average of 7.59%.  Additionally, our method successfully achieves 81.5% accuracy on the multi-NLI dataset with the added difficulty of only using 1% of the original training data, a result that outperforms BERT by 11.6%.  The benefits of our approach are further highlighted by an evaluation of human-generated annotations on 11 datasets, indicating a 6.85% average improvement in accuracy when compared to standard BERT.  By combining our method with the strong semantic capabilities of Completets, a model that complements the sequence-based capabilities of BERT, we achieve notable gains of 10.3% and 5.8% on the QA and Sentiment Analysis datasets, respectively.  The effective use of word meanings within the vector space allows our approach to successfully generalize words, a capability that is then leveraged to counter the lexical gap issue in AML.  To facilitate further research, we make the code, training data, and results publicly available.  Ultimately, our results demonstrate the significant promise of vector-space-based language models to overcome the lexical gap issue affecting BERT-like models. However, implementing large antenna arrays on mobile devices is challenging due to space and cost constraints. This research introduces a novel approach using a low-rank approximation technique to minimize the number of required antennas while precisely mimicking the behavior of a full-size antenna array. By utilizing a $64$-antenna array equivalent to a $256$-antenna array in terms of performance, our method shows significant improvements in data rates and reduces strong non-line-of-sight (NLOS) throughput gaps by up to $60\%$. Furthermore, the antenna size reduction is shown to be performance-transparent even in multi-user scenarios and supports a wide range of bandwidths from $100$MHz to $10$GHz. Real-world deployments of this approach are also demonstrated through the use of a 5G testbed at the University of Nebraska-Louisiana, showing notable improvements in end-to-end system performance. The proposed technique is a powerful tool for enhancing wireless system performance, addressing space and cost limitations, across various frequency bands and use cases. The achieved reduction in antenna density, however, may worsen the problem of radio frequency (RF) chain throughput, which is not addressed in this research. Moreover, the technique's performance relies heavily on sophisticated machine learning algorithms requiring substantial computational resources, which might hinder deployment on edge devices. Nevertheless, the technique exhibits great promise for future wireless systems, and further research is needed to overcome its current limitations. The model captures the rise and stabilization of a high-voltage, quasi-dc discharge consisting of two parts: a linear propagation region, and a non-linear reaction zone where a shock wave forms. The model shows that the discharge's stability is determined by a specific linear system representing the propagation region, and that this system dictates the stability of the entire discharge. The model also provides a new perspective on previous studies of discharge stability. Additionally, conditions are derived to prevent the discharge from becoming unstable and to minimize the time it takes for the discharge to stabilize. These conditions involve limiting the current at the short-circuit point to prevent the discharge from becoming unstable, and to ensure the discharge stabilizes quickly, the equivalent capacitance must be small, and the inductance can be either small or large depending on the resistance and capacitance values. These conditions also provide a physical understanding of discharge stability and can be verified experimentally. This analysis lays the groundwork for a general study of linear dynamical models for discharge phenomena. Finally, the model is applied to a specific configuration of the Venetian-blind discharge, and the results show excellent agreement with experimental data. This analysis highlights the importance of considering the nonlinear reaction zone in discharge phenomena and provides a framework for analyzing other discharges using similar models. The model's ability to predict unstable discharges and stabilization times holds promise for optimizing discharge designs. Further investigation is planned to explore the venus discharge in detail, as well as other discharges with similar models. The model's code is included for convenience. This requires a thorough examination of a specific discharge configuration, involving both theoretical modeling and experimental data comparison, to establish a common foundation for future optimization strategies. By training a new model on stolen data from a stronger model, an attacker can significantly reduce the difference in performance between their own model and the stolen one.  This paper reveals that even with highly confidential and heavily regulated datasets such as medical records, the underlying features and patterns can be extracted from a stolen model by exploiting existing evaluation tools. By analyzing the decisions made by the stolen model during common assessment tasks, the attacker can isolate distinctive characteristics in the output probability distributions.  By combining this understanding with subsequent processing of the raw data from the stolen model, the attacker can obtain a compressed representation of the original input, resulting in a notable improvement in performance.  Notably, this technique only demonstrates a 6% gain in performance on medical images, suggesting that model stealing attacks through this method may face difficulties when applied to such complex visual data.  By contrast, the same approach yields a 260% increase in performance on medical classification tasks involving less complex images, such as those found in the MIMIC-III dataset.  A further observation is that this attack is most effective on data with relatively simple underlying features, such as text and incremental medical classification.  Measures to prevent model stealing attacks are also explored, including introducing random variations in the stolen model's output during common assessment tasks, thus obscuring the underlying features and patterns.  This approach is found to be an acceptable compromise between performance and security, resulting in a negligible decrease in model performance following this modification.  Consequently, this strategy presents a viable solution for enterprises looking to protect their AI technology from model stealing attacks.  This approach is reusable across various models and datasets, thus providing a general framework for public institutions and private companies to safeguard their machine learning models against such threats.  Furthermore, this technique may also serve as a precursor to detecting unauthorized model access, by identifying unusual patterns in model evaluation metrics during regular assessment cycles.  This could in turn enable the detection of model stealing attacks before they produce tangible gains in performance, thus providing early warning indicators for such threats. By starting a conversation with the original statements of source A against source B, we can determine the positions of all parties involved. To address this, we've established a categorization of metric spaces based on their convex subsets' simplicity, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the generalized spaces' geometry.  This involves analyzing the accessibility of points in these spaces and the geometric shape of their convex subsets.  Seven distinct categories of metric spaces are identified, with examples including the real numbers, Euclidean spaces, and spaces of continuous functions.  Furthermore, we've developed a method to classify spaces based on their convex subsets, and this classification is shown to be deterministic.  The theory also applies to spaces with a more complex geometry, like the space of continuous functions with the Banach-Mazur distance.  We've extended our results to spaces that can be reduced to a p-metric space, and we address questions related to the geometry of spaces that can be projected onto a p-metric space.  This research contributes to the broader understanding of the geometry of generalized metric spaces, building on previous work that focused on the geometry of spaces that can be reduced to an Euclidean distance space.  We've also introduced a new approach to defining the angle between subspaces of a generalized metric space, and this approach supports the characterization of spaces with an angle-preserving isometry. Despite its advantages over traditional local optimization methods, FWI often faces challenges due to its nonlinear nature and the need for precise initial models. One possible approach to address these limitations is to leverage the Bayesian Framework (BF), which accounts for data uncertainty and models the parameter field as a probability distribution. However, implementing BF in real-world scenarios is complicated by the large parameter space and the requirement for real-time inverse solutions. This research introduces an online Bayesian Inference algorithm that utilizes the PyAMG library for linear algebra operations and the UBC Fullwave Formulation for seismic wavefield propagation. By incorporating the Gaussian Process (GP) as a parametrization for the frequency-domain wavefield, this algorithm reduces the dimensionality of the model. Although GP has been applied in 1-D statics correction, this research extends its use to 3D FWI. The results show that the GP-based approach achieves comparable accuracy to traditional methods to 4-5 digits and outperforms them when considering the dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, this algorithm allows for the incorporation of multiple data sets by combining data weights via GP, eliminating the need for weighted averaging in traditional methods. By solving a typical Eurasia model with two data sets, this algorithm demonstrates its ability to recover accurate models while correctly identifying data contamination. The computational cost of this algorithm varies between 150-300 GB of RAM and approximately 500-600 hours for a typical Eurasia model on 128 CPUs. By leveraging distributed memory using the Memory Scalable Framework, this algorithm achieves a memory reduction of up to 12 times. Consequently, this implementation is now capable of processing models with a resolution of 50m. Ultimately, this research provides a feasible solution for real-world 3D FWI problems involving high-resolution models and extensive data sets. Although the current version has computational and memory limitations, it serves as a starting point for further optimizations, such as linearity approximation, structure learning, and memory-intensive problems using distributed memory. Moreover, this research introduces the Data-rich Inverse Problems Challenge (DIPC) benchmark dataset, comprising synthetic data sets suitable for 3D Fullwave Formulation Inversion. To investigate this inquiry, we created an innovative framework called the Adversarial Galton Board, an adaptation of the classic Galton Board, a pioneering benchmark for studying and demonstrating the concept of "generalizing" in adversarial conditions.  Our framework consists of a comprehensive suite of tests that evaluate a model's ability to generalize its defenses across various domains.  These tests are supported by a suite of metrics that provide in-depth analysis of a model's generalization capabilities.  Our results show that existing state-of-the-art methods fall short of developing a truly general robust model, as confirmed by our framework and metrics.  Our findings particularly highlight the vulnerability of these methods to multi-domain attacks and the limitations of their adaptive training.  To address these issues, we propose an advanced multi-domain training approach called CoarseCorr, a technique that refines multiple correlations simultaneously.  Our results demonstrate that CoarseCorr yields a general robust model, as validated by our framework and metrics, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in this domain.  Our approach significantly improves generalization, as evidenced by GMCorr, a metric introduced for the first time, which measures generalization based on correlation.  Our research also introduces the concept of a Generalization Correlation Matrix (GCM), a metric that provides in-depth analysis of generalization, opening up possibilities for further research and advancements in this area.  Our results also suggest that generalization can be achieved through the development of a universal defense strategy applicable to all models, as confirmed by our framework and metrics, an outcome with major implications for the field of adversarial machine learning.  Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive suite of tests and analysis that can be applied to evaluate the generalization capabilities of a model's defenses, a crucial requirement for further advancements in this area. associated with always-on camera and microphone access in smart home devices. A novel attack has been devised that takes advantage of the delayed activation of these devices' security protocols. The attack occurs when a user is coerced into allowing an attacker temporary physical access, enabling the attacker to briefly activate the device and gain permanent access. A theoretical model of this attack has been developed and analyzed in a virtual environment. Our findings demonstrate that this type of attack is feasible against popular smart home devices, including those with voice control functionality. Additionally, various preventive measures were tested and evaluated for their effectiveness in preventing the attack. A proposed mitigation strategy involves delaying the device's secure boot time relative to when the user grants access. However, our results indicate that stretching the device's secure boot time may not sufficiently prevent the attack. Consequently, the most effective approach in preventing the attack is to require the user to enter their authentication credentials during the physical access window. It is also advisable for users to be aware of the devices they grant temporary access to and to maintain the security of their own credentials. Finally, providers of smart home devices should inform users about the delayed activation period of the security protocols and suggest users employ the devices' local interfaces rather than remote access for critical tasks. To resolve this ambiguity, we've developed a technique to measure a demon's information density and demonstrated that it inevitably increases as the sorting process continues. This implies that a demon could sort particles at a rate proportional to its own information density, but only up to the point where its information density equals that of the surrounding heat bath. From this, we've derived the maximum efficiency with which a demon can sort particles, and found it to be in proportion to the difference between the entropy densities of the sorted and unsorted regions. Surprisingly, we've discovered that a demon can sort particles even when the two regions are in thermal equilibrium with each other. As an example, we've simulated a demon sorting particles in three-dimensional free space, and observed its behavior as it sorts particles in various scenarios, including when the regions are out of equilibrium, and when the system is more complex, such as when sorting between two different types of regions, or when those regions are moving. By analyzing how extensions of neural networks leverage connected substructures in images, we develop a theoretical framework that utilizes graph concepts to model and assess the robustness of these networks.  Specifically, we create a language for describing graph-embedded data and propose a framework that evaluates the robustness of neural networks in relation to the structure of the data they're trained on.  We then use this framework to investigate two phenomena:  how neural networks prioritize individual image features when they're connected, and how the model's robustness is affected by these features.  Our results show that the features most valued by the network are those that provide the highest degree of support, but this can sometimes lead to a situation where a weakly-supported feature significantly lowers the model's robustness.  We also find that the network's preference for features is heavily influenced by its primary choice, and that this preference can be seen as a form of hierarchy where more strongly-supported features are preferred over those that are less supported.  We demonstrate the practical application of our framework by testing it on a series of models trained on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.  The code for our experiments is available at the end of this paper.  We show that by analyzing the underlying structure of the data, slight modifications can be made to significantly improve the robustness of the model, and that these modifications target specific features in the images.  For example, on the CIFAR-10 dataset, the default ResNet-56 model achieves a test accuracy of 72.5%, but by accounting for the structure of the data, we were able to enhance the robustness of the model, ultimately achieving a test accuracy of 79.5% without modifying the network itself.  We attribute this improvement to an increase in the network's ability to recognize hierarchical features, and to a greater imbalance in its preference for features that are more strongly supported.  We demonstrate the practical application of our framework to a series of tasks, and show that by analyzing the structure of the data, the robustness of the model can be improved, and that this improvement is largely the result of the network learning to recognize hierarchical features.  We also provide an interpretation of the hierarchy preferred by the network that can be applied to real-world images, and we show that this hierarchy captures intuitive patterns of organization in natural visual data. As a solution, this work introduces the concept of "concurrent specification specifications" (CSS), which is a higher-order abstract syntax (HOAS)-based description of the desired concurrent behavior of a library. Although the significance of these connections is widely acknowledged, the precise manner in which they affect the comprehension of sequential information within language is not well understood.  To investigate this question, a series of psychological experiments was designed to examine the role of sequential structure in the comprehension of speech.  The results of these experiments revealed that the way in which we arrange the connections between isolated elements of language affects the ease with which the sequence can be logically deduced, independent of the structure of the elements themselves.  Additionally, the data showed that the ease of deriving the sequence's logical implications is a critical factor in determining how easily the sequence can be mentally visualized.  However, the experiments did not provide sufficient support for the hypothesis that the ease of deriving the sequence's logical implications directly influences its semantic meaning.  A significant outcome of our study is that the comprehension of sequential information within language is best represented by a theory known as Montague's PCF, combined with a technique for predicting the ease with which the resulting intensional types can be mapped to meaningful propositions that depend on the sequence's logical implications and its ability to be mentally visualized. a brain, in comparison to the complex structure of the network itself, is still an area that requires further research. Although the brain's network topology is intricately detailed, the interconnectivity map, also known as the connection strength matrix, is not fully resolved at a level that matches the network's graph representation. This limitation holds true even for the well-studied mouse brain. Our research introduces an innovative method for reversing the direction of inference between network architecture and topology. By utilizing a data-driven approach that incorporates the non-locality principle, we can recover the interconnectivity map from the network architecture. The architecture is defined as the set of node features that pinpoint the locations, properties, and identities of neurons and glial cells within the brain. The data employed stems from the publicly available C-CMAP dataset, which comprises maps of cell features obtained through histology across various brain regions of a mouse. The recovery of the connection strength matrix was validated through synthetic network generation and tested against real-world data. The results show that our method is both efficient and accurate in recovering the mouse brain's interconnectivity map. Moreover, we were able to recover a level of detail in the map that previous attempts have not achieved. This implies that the topology of the mouse brain's network is intricate, featuring a high degree of node connectivity that is in line with recent studies on network architecture. By reversing the direction of inference, our research also enables the exploration of a longstanding hypothesis: if the architecture of a brain network is known, can the topology be deduced? To answer this question, we constructed two networks with identical architecture but distinct topologies. The hypothesis is supported by data showing that the map recovered from the architecture of these networks matches their topological characteristics. This finding has significant implications, suggesting that the architecture of a brain network encodes the rules necessary to generate its topology. Additionally, we provide evidence that a specific architectural feature, namely the distribution of neuron membrane area across brain regions, is sufficient to predict regional connectivity probabilities. This discovery sheds new light on previous studies of regional connectivity distributions. Furthermore, we were able to recover a detailed map of connectivity probabilities, enhancing understanding of the mouse brain's connectivity. This research focuses on developing a unified, high-speed method for evaluating the dependability of road, air, and sea transportation systems. A novel, compact representation of transportation networks is created using an electrical impedance model, allowing for rapid computation of reliability probabilities. By leveraging the impedance model's properties, the network is divided into disjoint subsets that can be processed independently to determine overall network reliability. The proposed method's efficiency is demonstrated through comparisons with traditional Monte Carlo simulation methods, yielding significant performance improvements (up to 500 times faster) with comparable accuracy. The reliability evaluation algorithm has been implemented in an open-source software tool and applied to real-world case studies involving transportation networks in Guam and the Port of Seattle. The results show that the program can handle large networks with hundreds of thousands of possible system states, showcasing its capability to provide rapid reliability assessments for complex transportation systems. Furthermore, the method has the potential to be adapted for other critical infrastructure networks. The code is available upon request from the authors. for undirected graphs. Undirected graphs can be represented as an $n$-by-$n$ matrix,
where the entry at row $i$ and column $j$ contains the message sent from node $i$
to node $j$. We analyze the memory requirements of the algorithms by considering the
maximum memory needed to store messages for a single node. Similarly, the total memory
needed across all nodes is represented as the maximum memory sum over all nodes,
which is equivalent to the maximum matrix row sum. Some algorithms demonstrate fixed
memory usage per node, while others exhibit variable memory requirements depending
on the graph structure. We identify specific clustering tasks and examine the memory
usage patterns for 3-node, 4-node, and 5-node graphs. Notably, the Degree-Centrality
algorithm shows degree-dependent memory usage, whereas the Betweenness-Centrality and
Closeness-Centrality algorithms display memory usage correlated with the number of
neighbors each node has. The Close Approximation algorithm exhibits degree-dependent
memory usage as well. We observe that some memory usage patterns conform to established
analytical formulas, whereas others require additional mathematical expressions.
The Cytoscape Java app 'ClusterAnalyzer' is available for public download and can
be used to examine memory usage patterns for a given graph and clustering algorithm.  This work lays the foundation for a future project that will aim to minimize memory usage during clustering processes. Network has been gaining interest in recent years as an efficient way to reconstruct evolutionary relationships. This type of network can accurately capture the connections between species over time, despite being less common than tree structures in current applications. Existing methods for building phylogeny networks are restricted to general types of structures and do't take into account the characteristics of the data at hand. In contrast, our proposed approach is a supervised algorithm that's specific to genomic data and can build a robust phylogeny network even for distantly related species. Our model's key feature is a set of edge types, each representing a different type of evolutionary mechanism, that's used to optimize a scoring function under the constraint of semibinary structure. To train and evaluate our model, we've developed a new set of metrics, including a method for calculating the area under the curve for partial ROCs. According to our results, our model consistently outperforms a state-of-the-art comparative genomics method on a wide range of organisms. Furthermore, a smaller-scale analysis involving primates and a side study on cancer genomes have shown that the types of evolutionary mechanisms encoded in our model are closely related to known genomic characteristics, such as gene families and pathway operations. Additionally, our model has identified distinct mechanisms across different species and taxonomic groups, also indicating that different types of evolutionary mechanisms are often found together in the same genome. Lastly, our model and all of its data are available for public use. By accurately capturing the diversity of evolutionary mechanisms, our model provides a strong foundation for further research in comparative genomics and phylogeny networks. This will enable us to better understand the underlying mechanisms of evolutionary change, spot signatures of recent gene exchange, and study the evolution of genomic characteristics that are involved in the development and progression of diseases. Moreover, our model's ability to reconstruct robust phylogeny networks will allow us to efficiently infer the evolutionary relationships between distant species and pinpoint regions of the genome that are most relevant to our inquiry. This will be especially beneficial for further analysis using other tools, such as alignment and comparative genomics methods, as well as for downstream applications like data imputation and genetic trait prediction. This will also be helpful for streaming genomic data by first using our model to reconstruct the evolutionary relationships and then using other tools on those results. Additionally, we identify another family of genus-one curves with a constant complexity, described by the equation $y^2 = x^3 - ax^2 - 6x - 9$, which is a quadratic twist of the previous family. Both of these families have infinite numbers of curves for which the coefficients are integers. This method may be applied to any genus-one curve defined by $y^2 = f(x)$, where $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $d$. The estimated complexity of such a genus-one curve is approximately $O(d^5)$ when computed over the rational numbers. This paper also presents theoretical evidence that the complexity of a genus-one curve defined by $y^2 = f(x)$ is upper bounded by $O(d^7)$ when computed over a finite field of a given size. This research provides a solution to a problem posed by Sullivan.

These methods typically assume that the movement of an optical meteor is described by a parametric two-dimensional function, and they utilize a mathematical model to derive the parameters from multiple images of the meteor. A common approach to creating this function is to use a catmull-rom spline, which requires that the control points are converted from three-dimensional space to two-dimensional projection coordinates. These conversion calculations are often skipped or approximated in meteor science literature. This paper discusses the derivation of the conversion calculations in question and presents a comprehensive overview of the subsequent parameter estimation techniques used in the field. We also demonstrate the utility of our explanation by employing an innovative method, known as the direct method, which avoids the use of catmull-rom splines and related conversion calculations. The direct method is shown to be a viable alternative for estimating the trajectory of optical meteors. The proposed direct method can be applied to any optical video analysis system, and the results indicate that it yields comparable accuracy to the traditional approach. Furthermore, the direct method has the added benefit of being more robust to image noise and artifacts. The technique is demonstrated through the application of three well-known meteor video datasets. The code used for the experiments is also made available online. The discussion section explores potential applications and future developments for the direct method. Additionally, concerns about the issue of meteor disintegration are discussed and a solution to this problem is presented. This solution involves tracking the core of the meteor rather than the entire disintegrated body. It is shown that the proposed direct method is capable of identifying the core and successfully estimating the trajectory of the meteor core. It is also demonstrated that the core generally accounts for at least half of the apparent brightness of the meteor. Based on this finding, a criterion is established to determine whether the traditional method or the direct method should be employed. It is agreed that methods such as the one presented in the paper are needed to accurately model the trajectories of large and bright meteors. This is because annotation processes that involve both reading and writing, such as generating text based on images, are resource-intensive and costly.  To streamline the dataset creation process, we are proposing a novel approach that leverages large amounts of unannotated data.  Our approach combines two existing techniques: one that uses text similarities to generate new training data from existing labeled data on a specific topic, and another that utilizes free-form writing to produce high-quality, diverse text. Notably, this model incorporates a mechanism of social influence that affects how agents' preferences are perceived by others. We demonstrate that, under a condition of strategic disclosure, the most profitable outcome for the majority voter can be achieved through a mechanism of social influence that induces agents to truthfully reveal their preferences. Moreover, we examine how the model of strategic disclosure interacts with a variety of voting systems, including Plurality, Condorcet, and Borda, and we investigate the impact of diverse coalition formations on the outcome. Our findings specifically consider situations where agents form coalitions based on their private preferences or where they do so randomly. We show that under Plurality voting and random coalition formation, the outcome that maximizes the benefit to the majority voter can be achieved through a mechanism of social influence that induces agents to truthfully disclose their preferences. However, under Condorcet and Borda voting, particularly with diverse coalitions, the outcome that maximizes the benefit to the majority voter may not be achievable through a mechanism of social influence that induces truth-telling.  Finally, we compare our model of influence to another model described in a prior study, and we demonstrate that under certain conditions and types of voting, the two models result in identical strategic behaviors for agents.  Our analysis ultimately highlights the significance of accounting for both strategic behavior and social influence in elections.  We also identify a research gap in elections that involves multiple agents with diverse preferences, particularly in areas such as committee formation and Suisse-style voting systems.  We offer an approach for addressing this gap through the application of game theory in combination with network influence models.  We present an approach for analyzing equilibrium outcomes in these types of elections through the use of an extended Shapley value, and we demonstrate this approach through the application of SUISSE, a system for studying strategic behavior in multi-agent elections. Previously, the cylindrical contact homology of a special type of tight contact structure on a 3-sphere with a link that includes a trefoil knot was calculated in the literature. Our research allows us to generalize this result to a wider class of links. The algorithm we develop to achieve this end is a key contribution of the paper and may be useful in computing homology for other types of links. The method involves modifying Trudinger's original approach to defining a Sobolev space that is suitable for the cylinders used in cylindrical contact homology. The modification is based on Ni's more advanced analysis of the Sobolev embedding theorem. The result we obtain includes the detection of nontrivial Reeb orbits as well as the computation of the homology of the cylindrical contact manifold for a link that includes a trefoil knot. The algorithm also reveals that the cylindrical contact homology of the standard link is zero. The method we employ to prove this result is an alternative to the one proposed by Murphy. The proposed method involves demonstrating that the boundary operator associated with the cylindrical contact homology is nilpotent by showing that it squares to zero. The argument we present to achieve this end is based on a key lemma that ensures a specific set of orbits is preserved by the boundary operator. The lemma's proof relies on Ghiggini's argument that a point on a sphere can be connected to a point in a lower-dimensional plane only if the sphere's contact structure is equivalent to the standard contact structure on the sphere. The lemma's other condition, which states that none of the cylinders used in the computation have a structure that is equivalent to the standard contact structure, is already known from previous research. The proposed method also involves verifying that the cylindrical contact homology satisfies the expected properties of a functor. The result we obtain is stored in a database that is accessible online. The database contains not only the cylindrical contact homology of the standard link but also the homology of the tight contact structure determined by the bridle link, which includes a trefoil knot, as well as the homology of the tight contact structure determined by the Whitehead link. The database further contains the nontrivial Reeb orbits of the tight contact structure determined by the bridle link, which includes a trefoil knot, as well as the nontrivial Reeb orbits of the tight contact structure determined by the Whitehead link.

Due to limitations of available data, particularly for isotopes around the stability line, a new experiment at the MESSAS facility in Mexico plans to measure neutron skin thickness for various isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, magnesium, phosphorus, and sulfur.  This experiment will involve measuring elastic scattering cross-sections resulting from the interaction of 1.79 GeV mesons with isotopes, with a specific emphasis on selecting targets and scintillator arrays to optimize detection efficiency and accuracy.  Prior to implementation, these plans will be reviewed in the context of the proposed experiment, with results to be measured informing theoretical models of dense matter and their corresponding predictions on the properties of heavy isotopes.  The experiment's expected outcomes, along with relevant background processes and the accuracy of meson scattering data, will also be discussed.  Due to the high energy involved (1.79 GeV), the detected events will primarily consist of elastic scattering and few-body breakup processes, with negligible contribution from other processes.  This has been validated through GENIE generator simulations, with results indicating that for isotopes around the stability line, the detected events will be 99.9% elastic scattering, with the remaining 0.1% consisting of three-body breakup processes.  Similarly, for isotopes with large neutron excess, the detected events will be 99.7% elastic scattering, with the remaining 0.3% consisting of two-body breakup processes. Ultimately, the results from this experiment along with further research involving other detection methods will provide a comprehensive understanding and precise measurement of neutron skin thickness for the mentioned isotopes.  This measurement will then be used to constrain theoretical models of matter within the nucleus. This research introduces an online, multi-stage version of the 0/1 knapsack problem, where binary items arrive one by one, and we must make binary decisions for each item independently, given all previous choices. Each item has a weight, a value, and a deadline, representing the latest stage by which it can be accepted. We can accept an arrived item before its deadline, but its value becomes zero. We aim to maximize total value within each stage and across all stages, subject to a dynamic knapsack capacity that depends on weights of accepted items. Since public interactions are often influenced by random events beyond control, accounting for this variability is essential to assess their impact. To do this, researchers typically use statistical methods to compare outcomes under controlled conditions, such as randomized experiments or statistical modeling of naturally occurring data. The choice of method depends on the design of the study, data availability, and the underlying structure of the data. This paper focuses on statistical modeling for randomized public engagements, specifically when data follows a normal distribution. It reviews commonly used methods, including ANOVA, linear regression, and mixed effects models, to help readers choose between them. Ultimately, the paper aims to educate readers on common statistical modeling approaches and their applications in a randomized setting. Since public engagements are often influenced by multiple factors, such as pre-existing conditions and new interventions, the paper also discusses how to construct effective models in these situations. It also provides guidance on how to diagnose model shortcomings and address them through modifications, such as adding or removing variables, which can be useful in similar policy-relevant research contexts. This paper is an extension of an article published in the Journal of Policy Analysis Management.

It covers the key characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages of ANOVA, linear regression, and mixed effects models. The paper also includes diagnostic tools to assess the validity of these models. It concludes by highlighting the importance of statistical modeling in a randomized setting and providing readers with a resource to choose between common modeling approaches.

Despite significant advancements, MT systems often fail to replicate human translation quality, a problem particularly pronounced when translating rare or out-of-domain texts. This concern stems from the inherent lack of transparency and reliability in many modern ML models, particularly those falling under black box categories. Such models, despite demonstrating impressive performance, raise critical questions about their decision-making processes and predictions, rendering them completely incomprehensible to users and stakeholders. Furthermore, the inability to grasp the inner workings of these models raises significant risks during their deployment, such as being prone to manipulation and producing wildly inconsistent results. To tackle this problem, researchers have been exploring ways to make ML models more transparent and interpretable, with a focus on understanding the features responsible for their predictions. This effort has given rise to a diverse range of explainable AI techniques, such as feature importance, partial dependence plots, and SHAP values, among others. As a result, researchers have been compelled to resort to bespoke solutions tailored to their specific problems, necessitating considerable effort and resources. Given the success of neural networks in numerous applications,  it is not surprising that they are frequently chosen for high-stakes classifications,  such as diagnosing life-threatening diseases or assessing social security disability claims.  However, there are growing concerns about the reliability and explainability of these models.  Research has shown that, in certain cases, neural networks can produce inconsistent results and prioritize accuracy over robustness.  For instance, they have been known to be easily manipulated into producing desired outputs by an adversary who can alter the input,  thus casting a shadow of doubt over the validity of any classification made by these models.  Furthermore,  efforts to gain insight into how these models make predictions have been met with limited success,  with most approaches focusing on validating model components rather than delving into the details of individual predictions.  Our study addresses these issues by introducing a new measure of a classifier's robustness,  which quantifies its resistance to manipulation and distinguishes it from its accuracy.  We then present a method for comprehending individual predictions,  which enables us to assign responsibility to both the model and the data.  Our findings reveal alarming rates of both high-stakes classification and prediction comprehensibility,  with model robustness trailing both.  To improve the robustness and comprehensibility of classifications,  we recommend a set of best practices,  which involve limiting data to prevent duplication and anamorphy,  diversifying training datasets,  using complaint data to train models,  thoroughly testing model robustness,  seeking human evaluation and validation,  treating medical and non-medical applications equally,  avoiding over-reliance on models in high-stakes classifications,  seeking second opinions,  which can be provided for free,  and providing insight into individual predictions.  Our study serves as a call to action for the machine learning and data research communities to address these issues jointly.  We also invite organizations considering using machine learning in the United States to fill out our robustness checklist.  Our goal is to create a national strategy to make machine learning more robust and comprehensible,  which will underpin a new era of trustworthy classification in the country. The Jones polynomial was initially proposed by V. Jones in 1989 as an operator invariant within the context of the von Neumann algebras associated with a link diagram. Its connection to the planar algebra $P$ established by P. Barram enables the computation of the Jones polynomial from a given link diagram using the quantum spin networks, and this computation can be performed efficiently with the help of the computer program Mathematica.

The knot determinant, on the other hand, is an algebraic knot invariant that can be derived from the Chern-Simons gauge theory proposed by E. Witten. This invariant is a complex number associated with each knot or link, and it has the property of distinguishing non-isomorphic knots or links. The knot determinant can also be represented through the quantum invariant known as the Witten zeta function, which is a complex number function associated with each knot or link.

The talk will focus on both the knot determinant and the quantum invariant known as the Witten zeta function, as well as their connection to the Jones polynomial, with an emphasis on explaining how they can be computed from a given link diagram using the computer program Mathematica. Additionally, the talk will also cover the application of the knot determinant and the Witten zeta function in distinguishing non-isomorphic knots or links, with specific examples including the trefoil knot and the figure-of-eight knot, as well as the links known as the Hopf link and the link with three components comprising a trefoil knot and a Hopf link component. The talk will also introduce the new concept of a modified Witten zeta function and demonstrate its ability to distinguish the trefoil knot and the figure-of-eight knot. The methods employed in the computation of both the knot determinant and the Witten zeta function are based on the representation of a given link diagram as a collection of inter-connected sub-diagrams known as the Ibrahimi-Barram sub-diagrams, and the computation of the quantum invariant known as the Kauffman polynomial from each of these sub-diagrams. This understanding of 109 degrees domain wall physics may enable the development of high-sensitivity magnetic sensors utilizing DW memory cells, particularly in a SrTiO3 base where 109 degrees domain wall resistance can represent a notable fraction of the total resistance.  This concept is illustrated with an example of a Hall sensor integrated with a DW memory cell, allowing for switching the domain wall state to modulate the sensor's output, enhancing its sensitivity when detecting magnetic field changes in both down and up directions.  This Nb-doped SrTiO3 technology offers reduced material costs and simpler fabrication compared to AFM-based DW memory cell sensors, exhibiting a level of magnetic sensitivity comparable to state-of-the-art spin torque magnetic sensors, with a particular ability to detect changes in a static magnetic field.  This is particularly beneficial for the type of magnetic field found in human environments, but room temperature sensitivity is slightly decreased in comparison to STMTS, which can also be achieved with this method by reducing the active DW area through lithographic means, sacrificing some memory capacity. Existing approaches are typically centered around machine learning-based techniques that identify and neutralize backdoors.  This research introduces a different approach, shifting the focus from machine learning to algebraic properties of functions used in data modification.  We uncover an undesirable property of the activation mechanism used in typical backdoor designs.  Specifically, we identify that the fusion function used in conventional backdoor designs, which combines the target model and auxiliary functions, necessarily incorporates the original data in a manner that is irreversible.  This leads to the designation of this property as the "backdoor identity card."  We propose an alternative design framework that circumvents this property.  Furthermore, to rectify the algebraic distortion caused by the backdoor identity card, we introduce an approach to recover the distorted data.  This recovery approach can be applied universally, unaffected by the characteristics of the backdoor.  Based on this recovery and the proposed design framework, we devise a method to defend against diverse backdoors through data modification.  Experimental results demonstrate that this method is highly effective in removing backdoors of various types.  This approach also ensures that the clean model's performance is preserved post-deployment.  Ultimately, our proposed defense strategy provides a comprehensive solution to the diverse backdoor threat, achieving a balance between model integrity and performance. To address backdoor attacks comprehensively, a multi-faceted approach that integrates both machine learning and algebraic properties is necessary.   Research on team structure is often linked to other variables, yet the underlying relationship with
  project outcomes remains poorly understood and is in need of further exploration. This study
  utilizes data from 58 software development projects involving 183 teams, examining how team
  composition affects project outcomes. Our results reveal that team composition, specifically
  the distribution of primary and secondary developers, influences outcomes. However, the
  assigned project manager has no discernible effect on project outcomes. Additionally, the
  distribution of primary and secondary developers is not randomly assigned, instead being
  influenced by existing relationships between developers. These findings suggest that software
  development team composition is an interdependent mixture of critical and secondary
  members, and that outcomes are shaped by the distribution of these roles. The data also
  indicate that developers form relationships based on project composition, and that these
  relationships are formed before project assignment. These relationships are an underlying
  factor in project composition, shaping outcomes and influencing future relationships
  among developers. The name "Ripple" effect is proposed to describe this cycle of
  relationships, composition, assignment, and outcomes that repeats with each new project.
